@graph.headline: Monte Carlo Simulation for Traders: Ruin, Drawdown & Sizing

acceptedAnswer.text: Monte Carlo re-deals your actual trade-by-trade results — shuffled, skipped, execution varied — thousands of times, and the fan chart it builds is how you read median vs P10/P90 paths, the drawdown distribution, and your ruin probability. It prices sequence risk; it doesn't predict your future.

mainEntity.name: What is Monte Carlo simulation in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: A backtest shows one sequence: what your trades did in the exact order they happened to occur. Monte Carlo shows what those same trades could do across a thousand different orderings — backtesting estimates the edge, Monte Carlo estimates how bumpy the ride to that edge could be.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between backtesting and Monte Carlo simulation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Same as above: 1,000 as the working standard, 10,000 where tail estimates matter, ~100 for a rough read only.

mainEntity.name: How many Monte Carlo simulations should I run?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It assumes your trade sample represents the future and explores what different orderings of that sample could produce — if the sample is overfit or the regime changes, the fan's answers are conditional on a world that no longer exists.

mainEntity.name: Can Monte Carlo simulation predict future trading results?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — this is the garbage-in rule: Monte Carlo resamples the trades you give it, so validate out-of-sample first (how to detect overfitting) before putting the sample through the fan.

mainEntity.name: Does Monte Carlo work if my strategy is overfit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Run the fan at several risk-per-trade levels (e.g. 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 3%) and compare the ruin probabilities and 90th-percentile drawdowns, then pick the largest size whose worst plausible path you can genuinely survive. Use position sizing for the lot math and risk of ruin for the closed-form comparison.

mainEntity.name: How do I use Monte Carlo results to set position size?

acceptedAnswer.text: First define ruin — the account-loss line (say 30%) at which you'd stop trading the strategy. Practitioners often treat around 5% probability of crossing that line as roughly acceptable and more than 10% as a reason to avoid or resize. Those are third-party rules of thumb, not guarantees; the number only means something attached to a threshold you've truly committed to.

mainEntity.name: What is an acceptable probability of ruin?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because your backtest drew one lucky ordering of history. The fan explores orderings where losers cluster early and streaks stretch longer — sequences your sample contains but your single realized order happened to avoid. The worst paths aren't pessimistic; they're the honest price of the same trades dealt in a different order.
